summary: Flame in Freefall is an SI-powered web dashboard that turns decades of NASA microgravity combustion experiments into fire-safety insights for crewed space habitats. We unified 19 investigations from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database, including BASS, Saffire, SAME, FLEX and ACME, into one verified database of 1,533 tests, fixing and logging 181 data issues and checking it with 31 automated tests. The dashboard summarizes each investigation, ranks them for spacecraft, space stations, lunar and Martian bases and pressurized rovers, and interprets the data as six fire risks with evidence and recommendations for prevention, detection and suppression. It also provides modeling data, next-generation equipment insights, Earth applications, and an AI assistant that answers questions citing PSI IDs. This matters because future lunar habitats will use 30% oxygen or more, yet no solid material has been tested in microgravity above 22.2% oxygen, a critical gap our dashboard reveals.
details:
What it does and how it works
Flame in Freefall is an SI-powered web dashboard that summarizes, ranks and interprets NASA microgravity combustion research to deliver fire-safety insights for crewed space habitats. We downloaded the experimental tables of 19 investigations from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database (BASS, BASS-II, Saffire I–III, SAME, SAME-R, DAFT, FLEX, FLEX-2, CFI, SLICE, SPICE and six ACME experiments). A Python pipeline maps them into one schema with normalized units: fuel, sample shape and size, oxygen, pressure, airflow, diluent and outcome. The result is FireDB: 1,533 tests, with 181 data issues fixed and logged back to their source file and row, and 31 automated checks against the originals.

The dashboard includes:

  • An overview with filters, KPIs and charts.
  • Six fire risks, each with NASA evidence, a recommendation, the habitats it applies to and a data-confidence level.
  • Investigation rankings for spacecraft, space stations, lunar and Martian bases and pressurized rovers.
  • An oxygen–pressure map of every test, showing the lunar-base and spacesuit zones.
  • Investigation profiles, showing which variables changed between tests, and a side-by-side comparison tool.
  • Suppression analysis, next-generation equipment insights and Earth applications.
  • A modelers’ section with CSV, JSON and SQLite downloads and an example logistic model (AUC 0.816).
  • An AI assistant (Google Gemini, via a secure serverless function) that answers in English or Spanish using only FireDB, cites PSI IDs and says when data are missing.

Benefits
Engineers, researchers, professors and students can find, compare and interpret decades of NASA results in minutes instead of searching dozens of tables. Every number is traceable to NASA data.

Expected impact
The dashboard reveals a critical gap: future lunar habitats will use 30% oxygen or more, yet no solid material has been tested in microgravity above 22.2% oxygen. It points to the next experiments needed (solids at high oxygen and low pressure, partial-gravity data from LUCI and FM2) and supports safer material selection, detection and suppression in space and on Earth.

Tools
Python (pandas, scikit-learn, openpyxl), SQLite, HTML, CSS and JavaScript, GitHub, Netlify (hosting and serverless functions), the Google Gemini API, and Claude (Anthropic) as an AI coding and writing assistant. No hardware was used.

Creativity
We do more than display data: we verify it, turn it into risk cards and habitat rankings, and let anyone ask the data questions. Data-quality transparency is a feature in itself. A pixel-art llama mascot (AI-generated, labeled) adds an Andean identity from Ecuador.

Factors we considered

  • Data reliability and traceability.
  • Honest limits: trends versus causal results, and no partial-gravity data in PSI.
  • Risk levels presented as our interpretation, not NASA guidance.
  • AI safety: answers grounded in our data with citations, an API key never exposed, rate limits.
  • Accessibility: bilingual, light and dark modes, works on mobile.
  • Open access: public code and data.
